newsitem.title: USA: U.S. eying NZ as possible trade partner - envoy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. eying NZ as possible trade partner - envoy.

text.p: New Zealand, along with Australia and Singapore is one possible partner in future reciprocal trade agreements with the United States, the U.S. ambassador to New Zealand Josiah Beeman said on Tuesday.

Speaking at a corporate function in New York, Beeman noted that the U.S. trade representative's 1997 trade policy report raises, "the very interesting possibility of negotiating future reciprocal free trade agreements in the Asian Pacific and names New Zealand, Australia and Singapore as a few of our possible regional partners".
However, he added, it would be take a "hard sell" to get the Congress to agree to allow President Clinton the "fast-track" powers to instigate such agreements.
The ambassador said that the U.S. viewed New Zealand as a key partner in opening up markets to competition in the region.
"Bilaterally, 1996 ended with a bang in U.S.-New Zealand economic relations. One of the first acts of NZ's new coalition government was to agree to formally endorse the idea," he said.
"This was the first signal that the new National-NZ First coalition government lead again by Prime Minister Jim Bolger would not stray from NZ's free trade path.

"In the future New Zealand's new centre right coalition may pay more attention to their national interest in foreign investment decisions or to what NZ's major trading partners are doing to lower trade barriers as the government reviews its own tariff reduction plans," he went on.
"But I see no evidence that the new Bolger government has any intention of turning its back on 13 years of dramatic free market reforms."

After saying economic and security issues were closely linked in the Asia Pacific and noting America's on-going military presence in the region, Beeman indicated Wellington should reconsider its defence arrangements with the U.S..
He urged New Zealand to become "a full participant in regional efforts to guarantee peace and open trading routes."
He said APEC was under pressure to produce "concrete and measurable" results or risk losing the enthusiastic support of nations including the U.S..
Beeman quashed suggestions that APEC could develop into a NAFTA-like free trade bloc, but said the group continued to have the staunch support of U.S. President Bill Clinton.
"APEC is a vehicle to building consensus in the Asian Pacific," he said.
"I think that is the principal value of the forum of APEC -- I do not underestimate the difficulty of getting nations to agree to having their individual action plans.

"Only time will tell whether or not there is going to be one strong commitment to individual action plans ... what you can be assured of is that the US government will press for concrete results from APEC."

Replying to a question about President Clinton's future role in the forum posed by Robert Baume, Australia's consul general in New York, the ambassador expressed concern at the burgeoning bureaucracy surrounding APEC, "but we all realise the importance of continuing the momentum".
"I believe this President is fully committed to this process," he said. "He is a strong believer in free trade, sometimes perhaps to his political peril."
The ambassador was scheduled to head to Washington on Wednesday where he was playing a role in negotiations for a open skies aviation agreement between the United States and New Zealand.
